description: Team D&A is a group of curious, driven innovators united by a shared passion for space and technology. Combining skills in coding, data analysis, and design, we turn NASA's open data into creative, practical solutions for real-world problems. For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we're ready to collaborate, experiment, and build something that helps both Earth and the future of space exploration.
summary: When a lunar launch slips by a few days, teams must re-check sunlight and Earth visibility at their landing site. AILUNA turns NASA JPL Horizons-based ephemerides into an interactive comparison: choose a south-pole site or custom coordinates, a UTC landing date and mission duration, then explore Sun and Earth positions, visibility timelines, pinned scenarios and launch-delay alternatives. It helps mission planners, educators and the public understand the trade-offs between solar-energy opportunities and direct-to-Earth communication windows. Our prototype uses geometric visibility; local terrain and complete mission engineering constraints remain outside this model.
details:
AILUNA is an interactive web prototype for comparing lunar south-pole sites and landing dates. A launch delay can change both sunlight and Earth visibility; our linked horizon display, visibility timeline, comparison table, pinned scenarios and launch-delay exploration make those changes easy to examine. Users can enter custom coordinates, change UTC start time and mission duration, and export results.

The application uses precomputed hourly NASA JPL Horizons-based Sun and Earth positions and topocentric geometry. The documented model uses a 1737.4 km lunar sphere and a surface observer. Visibility means the object centre is above the geometric horizon. It does not include local terrain occlusion or guarantee a usable communication link or sufficient electrical power.

In one 14-day Malapert test beginning December 1, 2026, comparison against 336 hourly Horizons topocentric reference samples gave maximum elevation differences of approximately 0.006 degrees for the Sun and 0.001 degrees for Earth. This validates that scenario, not every location or mission constraint.

Built with web technologies, the prototype combines scientific data with an accessible visual interface for rapid exploration and education. NASA Moon Trek and LROC QuickMap were used as exploration references. Terrain-aware visibility and further site validation are future work.

AI disclosure: Codex and a teammate AI coding agent assisted code generation, debugging, research, interface development, validation and documentation. The team reviewed and integrated the resulting work.
